annotations.title: Alternating Harmonic Series (Mercator 1668)
annotations.content: The alternating harmonic series 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ⋯ = ln(2) is axiomatized because its proof requires Abel's theorem for boundary convergence of power series. The series is the Mercator series log(1+x) = x - x²/2 + x³/3 - ⋯ evaluated at x = 1, which is the boundary of the radius of convergence. Abel's theorem (1826) guarantees that if ∑aₙ converges, then lim_{x→1⁻} ∑aₙxⁿ = ∑aₙ.

annotations.title: Shifted Alternating Harmonic Series
annotations.content: The shifted series ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n+1) = 1 - ln(2) is obtained from the alternating harmonic series by an index shift. Starting from ln(2) = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ⋯, remove the first term (1) and negate: -(1/2 - 1/3 + 1/4 - ⋯) = -(ln(2) - 1) = 1 - ln(2). This is also axiomatized for the same reason: Abel's theorem at the boundary.

annotations.title: Partial Fraction Decomposition
annotations.content: The core algebraic step: for n ≥ 1, (-1)^{n+1} · 2/(n(n+1)) = 2·(-1)^{n+1}/n - 2·(-1)^{n+1}/(n+1). The proof uses funext (to reduce to pointwise equality), a case split on n = 0, then field_simp to clear denominators and ring to verify the resulting polynomial identity. The non-zero denominator conditions (n ≠ 0 and n+1 ≠ 0) are discharged by Nat.cast_ne_zero and positivity.

annotations.title: Series Algebra: mul_left and sub
annotations.content: After the partial fraction rewrite, the proof combines the two axiomatized HasSum results using Mathlib's series algebra. HasSum.mul_left scales a convergent series: if ∑aₙ = S, then ∑(c·aₙ) = c·S. HasSum.sub takes the difference: if ∑aₙ = S and ∑bₙ = T, then ∑(aₙ - bₙ) = S - T. The final arithmetic 2·ln(2) - 2·(1 - ln(2)) = 4·ln(2) - 2 is verified by ring.

annotations.title: Main Theorem: 4ln(2) - 2
annotations.content: The main result establishes HasSum for the alternating triangular reciprocal series with exact value 4·ln(2) - 2 ≈ 0.7726. The HasSum formulation (rather than tsum) is stronger: it asserts both convergence and the value of the limit. The n = 0 case is handled by mapping to 0 (since the formula 2/(n(n+1)) is undefined at n = 0), which is standard for series starting at n = 1 in Mathlib's ℕ-indexed framework.

annotations.title: Unscaled Corollary via const_smul
annotations.content: Derives the unscaled version ∑(-1)^{n+1}/(n(n+1)) = 2·ln(2) - 1 by dividing the main result by 2. The key technique is HasSum.const_smul with scalar 2⁻¹: if ∑(2·aₙ) = S, then ∑aₙ = S/2. The proof first rewrites the unscaled series as 2⁻¹ times the scaled series, then applies const_smul, and finishes with convert + ring.

annotations.title: Summability from HasSum
annotations.content: The series is summable, derived trivially from HasSum.summable applied to the main theorem. In Mathlib, HasSum f s implies Summable f — if a series converges to a specific value, it is summable. This is a one-line derivation.
annotations.mathContext: $\text{Summable}(n \mapsto (-1)^{n+1} \cdot 2/(n(n+1)))$ follows from the existence of the limit $4\ln 2 - 2$.

annotations.title: Oscillating Partial Sums
annotations.content: Four partial sums are computed by norm_num: S₁ = 1, S₂ = 2/3, S₃ = 5/6, S₄ = 11/15. These oscillate around the limit 4·ln(2) - 2 ≈ 0.7726, with odd partial sums above and even partial sums below — characteristic behavior of alternating series (Leibniz criterion). The oscillation demonstrates that the series converges slowly: after 4 terms, the error is still about |11/15 - 0.7726| ≈ 0.006.
annotations.mathContext: $S_1 = 1,\; S_2 = \frac{2}{3},\; S_3 = \frac{5}{6},\; S_4 = \frac{11}{15}$. The limit $4\ln 2 - 2 \approx 0.7726$ lies between each consecutive pair.
